takeaway: NanoFlow overlaps compute-, memory-, and network-bound LLM inference operations inside each GPU by scheduling profiled nano-batches, raising throughput when serving is compute-bound and heavily batched.
background: LLM inference mixes matrix multiplications, attention, and collective communication, each stressing different GPU resources. At large batches, the paper argues many evaluated models and workloads are compute-bound overall.
villain: Existing engines execute those heterogeneous operations sequentially within a device, leaving compute units idle between kernels even when each kernel uses its own bottlenecked resource well.
approach: NanoFlow divides a dense batch into independent nano-batches and overlaps nano-operations that bottleneck on different resources. A two-stage MILP search first chooses split sizes and ordering without interference, then uses profiled pairwise kernel interference to select resource allocations and kernel implementations. Its runtime forms mixed prefill/decode batches, executes the schedule with CUDA streams and events, and manages paged KV caches.
impact: The authors argue that this operation-level pipeline can move throughput-oriented LLM serving closer to a profiled compute ceiling without changing model semantics.

evaluation.overview: The authors measure offline throughput, latency under request traces, ablations, resource use, and schedule portability across dense and mixture-of-experts models.
evaluation.implemented: An end-to-end NVIDIA GPU serving runtime with custom CUDA kernels, automatic pipeline search, request scheduling, and hierarchical KV-cache management.
evaluation.setting: Primary tests serve FP16 LLaMA-2-70B on one DGX node with eight A100 GPUs using Splitwise, LMSYS-Chat-1M, ShareGPT, and fixed-length requests; additional models test schedule portability.

results.text: For request lengths drawn from Splitwise, LMSYS-Chat-1M, and ShareGPT, the authors report 1.91× average offline throughput versus TensorRT-LLM, the strongest system baseline in those tests.
In its LLaMA-2-70B offline tests, NanoFlow reaches 68.5% of the paper's profile-derived theoretical optimal throughput in the best case.

limitations: The paper's optimal-throughput analysis assumes the largest memory-fitting batch and applies to compute-bound workloads. A NanoFlow instance assumes abundant equal-priority requests, with autoscaling, load balancing, and priority routing outside the system.
phd_group_signal: This work signals a performance-systems style that combines analytical bottleneck modeling, kernel interference profiling, schedule search, and an end-to-end CUDA runtime.
beginner_concepts: GPU compute, memory, and network bottlenecks

claims.text: NanoFlow splits operations over independent nano-batches, overlaps nano-operations constrained by different GPU resources, and uses a two-stage search with measured interference to choose the pipeline and resource allocation.

The optimal-throughput model assumes the largest batch that fits model weights and KV caches, while each runtime instance assumes abundant equal-priority requests and delegates autoscaling, load balancing, and priority routing to an external control plane.
